description: Bilingual exchanges, period letters, songs and direct address to bring hidden histories to the stage.
content_html:
Language as Power on Stage

One of Tanika Gupta’s most distinctive dramatic methods in The Empress is her use of code-switching — moving between English, Bengali and Hindustani in the same conversation. This is not decorative. Every time a character shifts language, Gupta signals something precise: who holds power, who is excluded, and what a character guards as their own. When Rani and Mr Das speak Bengali to each other in the Lascar lodging-house scenes, the English characters in the room are shut out. The audience experiences, briefly, the same exclusion that Indian people experienced daily in Victorian Britain.

For a performer, delivering a bilingual scene demands close attention to accent and register. When Rani speaks to Mrs Wormwood, her English becomes careful, softened, deferential — lower pitch, measured pace, pauses before answering, a posture slightly inclined forward. The same actress playing the Lascar lodging-house scene can stand straighter, speak faster, a wider pitch range; her body reads the difference in status without the audience needing it explained.

Key Fact

The bilingual exchanges in The Empress work politically as well as theatrically: they remind the audience that English is the colonisers’ language, and that speaking it demands a performance of compliance from Indian characters. This is language as subtext — what is not said in English is as significant as what is.

Letters: Private Voices in Public History

Gupta uses epistolary staging throughout the play. Abdul Karim writes letters home to India; Rani struggles to find someone who will carry her words back across the ocean. A director staging these letter sequences faces a choice about staging configuration. In a theatre in the round configuration, a character reading a letter aloud becomes a private act watched by all — intimate and surrounded. In a proscenium arch configuration, a single spotlight isolating the letter-writer against a dark stage creates formality and distance, underlining the historical gulf between writer and reader.

The design possibilities for letter scenes are rich. A lighting designer might use a lighting special — a narrow profile spot — to hold the letter-writer in a pool of warm amber, suggesting both candlelight and memory. Sound could underpin these moments with a sparse Indian underscore: perhaps a single sitar phrase, unresolved, fading as the letter ends. The costume worn in letter scenes can be a design signal too: if Abdul writes home wearing both his Indian robes and a British-issued badge of office, the visual contradiction speaks volumes without a word.

Students sometimes argue that bilingual dialogue is simply there for historical authenticity — “they would have spoken Bengali in real life.” This loses marks. Gupta makes deliberate theatrical choices about when characters switch language and who is present. The dramatic question is always: what does the language shift do to the audience at this moment? Treat code-switching as a staging device with the same intentionality as a lighting change or a costume reveal.

Hindi Songs: the Brechtian Interrupt

Gupta includes Hindi songs and Indian music as a structural device. When the song interrupts the naturalistic action, the fourth wall becomes porous. This is a Brechtian effect: the emotional flow is paused; the audience is reminded it is watching a constructed history, not simply watching life. A sound designer staging the songs must decide whether the music comes from onstage musicians (diegetic — the characters can hear it too), from offstage (non-diegetic — felt but not seen), or from a recorded soundscape that places the song in the characters’ memory rather than their present.

A performer who delivers a Hindi song must choose whether to break eye contact with the other characters and address the audience directly. This is direct address: the character becomes a narrator of their own story. The physical choices here matter — does the performer stand still, commanding the stage? Or do they move through the space, making eye contact with audience members in different seats? Either choice communicates something about whether Rani (or Abdul) feels seen by the world watching them.

Key Fact

The songs in The Empress are not musical-theatre entertainment — they are political interruptions. Like the songs in Brecht’s epic theatre, they comment on the action rather than advancing it. They ask the audience to reflect on what they have just seen.

Direct Address and Victorian Registers

Gupta also contrasts the heightened formality of Victorian English court dialogue with the less formal registers of the Lascar lodging house and Rani’s scenes. When British court characters speak, their language is measured, ceremonially polite and opaque — meaning hidden behind etiquette. A performer playing Lord Salisbury or a courtier might adopt a clipped vocal quality: precise consonants, restrained volume, almost no pitch variation. The stillness is threatening. Contrast this with Rani’s scenes, where the dialogue can be direct, warmly colloquial, even comic — serving both character and political point. The audience roots for the more expressive voice.

Direct address is used particularly for Rani. When she steps forward and speaks to the audience, the staging must support this. A lighting designer might shift from the general lighting wash to a front-facing special, pulling her out of the scene. The sound designer might remove the ambient underscore entirely — silence framing her words. These design choices signal: this moment is outside the fiction; hear it differently.

As a performer: In the moment Rani first turns to address the audience from the Tilbury Docks scene, you might step forward from the tableau of the dock, pause for two full beats, make deliberate eye contact with a section of the audience — not a single person, but a sweep — then speak at a moderate pace with a slight raising of pitch on the key phrase, signalling that she is asking a question of the world, not just narrating. Your posture is upright but not rigid: dignity without defiance yet. Arms loose at your sides, hands slightly open. Proxemics matter: you place yourself downstage centre, separating yourself from the English family grouping behind you upstage.

As a designer: As the lighting designer you fade the general wash to 20% and bring up a single 650w profile spot from a front-of-house position, colour temperature a warm 2800K amber (suggesting both gaslight and a remembered warmth), no gobo. As the sound designer you drop the ambient dock soundscape (gulls, rigging, crowd murmur) to silence on her first step forward, replacing it with nothing — the silence itself becomes a sound cue that isolates her in time.
exam_tip_html: For the 12-mark question on playwright’s intentions, students commonly describe events — “Rani speaks Bengali to show she is Indian” — instead of analysing what Gupta wants the audience to think, feel or understand at that moment. The command word “analyse” demands you identify the intention, then explain how the dramatic method achieves it, then judge the effect on the audience. For a bilingual scene, a Mastering answer might argue: Gupta uses code-switching here to make the audience feel the discomfort of linguistic exclusion, placing them in solidarity with Rani rather than with the English family — a political alignment disguised as naturalistic detail. For extended-response questions, always anchor your analysis of language to a specific named moment of the play and show how a performer or designer could heighten that effect.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Code-switching between English, Bengali and Hindustani is a political device, not decoration — it signals power, exclusion and identity, and demands specific vocal and physical choices from performers.
  • Letters and direct address allow Gupta to give private voices a public stage — lighting specials, silence and a shift in proxemics can all signal these moments of testimony to the audience.
  • Hindi songs function as Brechtian interruptions: they pause the emotional flow and ask the audience to witness and reflect rather than simply feel.

practice_questions.text: Name the dramatic method Gupta uses when a character steps forward and speaks directly to the audience.
What is meant by code-switching in the context of The Empress?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that it involves moving between two or more languages; 1 mark for explaining its purpose — to signal power, identity, exclusion or cultural difference within a scene.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Gupta uses a Hindi song as a dramatic method to shape the audience's response to the Indian characters' situation.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that songs interrupt the naturalistic action (1); explanation that this creates a Brechtian distancing effect, preventing simple emotional absorption (1); reference to a named song moment in the play (1); explanation of how the audience is invited to reflect politically rather than just feel (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect on the audience when Rani moves from speaking English with Mrs Wormwood to speaking Bengali with Mr Das in the Lascar lodging-house scenes.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that the language shift signals a change in status and safety (1); explanation that English-speaking audience members experience Rani's exclusion from within the docks scene and then her inclusion in Bengali community (1); reference to how a performer could physically mark this shift (1); explanation of the political meaning this creates for the audience watching Victorian race and power dynamics (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in making Rani's letters home a central dramatic device in The Empress. Consider what Gupta wants the audience to understand about belonging, voice and the Indian experience in Victorian Britain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Candidate analyses multiple intentions behind the letter device (private testimony made public; the fragility of connection across empire; the contrast between official history and personal voice); anchors analysis to named moments of the play; explains the audience's likely emotional and political response; weighs how the staging of letters (direct address, design choices) amplifies Gupta's intentions; sustained throughout.

Secure: Candidate identifies two or more intentions and explains how the letter device serves them; refers to at least one named moment; some reference to staging or performer effect; generally accurate.

Developing: Candidate describes what letters show about Rani rather than analysing what Gupta intends the audience to think or feel; may retell elements of plot; intentions identified but not explored.

Emerging: Brief description of letters as a plot device; little or no analysis of playwright's purpose or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: You are directing The Empress for a GCSE Drama production. Discuss how you would stage the opening scene at Tilbury Docks, making specific choices about sound, lighting, costume and at least one performer, to communicate to the audience both the historical setting and the political situation Rani finds herself in. Refer to at least two design disciplines and one performer in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed, specific choices across two or more design disciplines (named sound cues with texture and source, lantern types with colour and direction, costume fabrics with cultural and class signals) and at least one performer (vocal quality, posture, proxemics, gesture at a named moment); every choice is justified with reference to what it communicates to the audience about the historical and political situation; staging choices are consistent and create a coherent directorial vision; reference to the contrast between Indian and English visual/aural registers on stage.

Secure: Choices made across at least two disciplines and one performer; generally specific (e.g. names a fabric or a sound type); most choices are justified; staging is mostly coherent.

Developing: Some design and performer choices offered but generic (e.g. 'period costumes', 'sad music'); limited justification; staging lacks coherent directorial vision.

Emerging: Lists ideas with little specificity or justification; description rather than analysis of staging effect.

knowledge_checks.q: What term describes a performer moving between two languages within the same scene?
When Gupta uses Hindi songs to interrupt the naturalistic action, this is best described as which type of dramatic effect?
options: Brechtian distancing — inviting reflection rather than pure emotion
A theatrical convention borrowed from musical theatre
An example of subtext communicated through song

knowledge_checks.q: When Rani steps forward to address the audience directly, this device is called _____.
A lighting _____ is a broad, even state covering the whole stage without strong directional shadows.
Match each dramatic method to its function in The Empress:
right: Signals power, exclusion and cultural identity between characters
Interrupts the action to invite political reflection — a Brechtian device
Brings a private voice into the public space of the theatre

flashcard_questions.a: Moving between two or more languages in a scene to signal power, identity or exclusion.
When a performer speaks to the audience rather than another character, stepping outside the fiction.
A single lantern isolating one performer while the rest of the stage is dark.
A broad, even light covering the whole stage with no strong directional shadow.
A layered atmospheric sound composition built from multiple audio elements.

flashcard_questions.q: What is underscore in sound design?
flashcard_questions.a: Non-diegetic music played quietly beneath dialogue to colour emotional atmosphere.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the fourth wall in theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: The imaginary boundary between stage and audience; breaking it reminds the audience they are watching theatre.
The spatial distance between performers on stage, communicating power, intimacy or status.

flashcard_questions.q: Who wrote The Empress and when did it premiere?
flashcard_questions.a: Tanika Gupta; it premiered at the RSC Swan Theatre in 2013.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a gobo in lighting design?
flashcard_questions.a: A metal or glass template placed in a lantern to project a pattern of light onto the stage.

flashcard_questions.q: What Brechtian effect do the Hindi songs in The Empress create?
flashcard_questions.a: They interrupt naturalistic flow, distancing the audience and inviting political reflection.
Letters written or spoken aloud on stage to reveal inner life or create dramatic irony.

glossary_terms.definition: Moving between two or more languages within a scene to signal power, identity or cultural exclusion.
When a performer speaks to the audience rather than to another character, stepping outside the fictional world.
A single lantern isolating one performer while the rest of the stage is dark or near-dark.
A broad, even lighting state covering the whole stage without strong directional shadows.
A layered atmospheric sound composition built from multiple audio elements to create the texture of a place or moment.
Non-diegetic music played quietly beneath dialogue to colour the emotional atmosphere of a scene.
The imaginary boundary between stage and audience; breaking it draws attention to the theatrical event itself.
The spatial distance between performers on stage, used to communicate power, intimacy, tension or status.
A metal or glass template placed in a lantern to project a pattern of light onto the stage.
